fact: National Jewish Health lists turf grass among five common Colorado allergens, names Kentucky bluegrass among the most common grass allergens, says grass usually pollinates in late spring and summer, and says high winds carry grass pollen for miles.
quote: Grass allergies are very common, and, if you’re trying to tend to your lawn or garden, this allergen is difficult to avoid. The most common grass allergens are the pollen from Bermuda, Johnson, Kentucky Blue, Sweet Vernal and Timothy grasses. Grass usually pollinates in the late spring and summer seasons. High winds will pull pollens into the air and carry them for miles.
source_label: National Jewish Health, 5 Common Colorado Allergens That Can Get in the Way of Gardening (published April 1, 2024)

fact: National Jewish Health says replacing turf grass with groundcovers or other plants you are not allergic to can reduce exposure, and that wearing a mask to mow, or having someone else mow, may help.
quote: Replacing turf grass with groundcovers or other plants you’re not allergic to can be a good way to reduce your exposure. Wearing a mask while mowing your lawn, or seeing if someone else can mow the lawn, might help decrease your symptoms.
source_label: National Jewish Health, 5 Common Colorado Allergens That Can Get in the Way of Gardening (published April 1, 2024)
notes: The page does not mention artificial turf; it suggests groundcovers or other plants. The guide says so.

fact: National Jewish Health says cottonwoods pollinate in spring, months before the cotton flies, and that symptoms while the cotton blows may be irritation from the cotton or an allergy to grass pollinating in summer.
quote: These are common in backyards everywhere and begin pollinating during in the spring. … Remember that cottonwood trees actually release their pollen months before the “cotton” begins to fly off the tree. … If you are having a flare-up of allergies when you see the “cotton” blowing around, you could be experiencing irritant-induced symptoms from the “cotton” or actual allergies from the grass that is pollinating during the summer months.
source_label: National Jewish Health, 5 Common Colorado Allergens That Can Get in the Way of Gardening (published April 1, 2024)
notes: "begin pollinating during in the spring" is the source's wording, quoted as printed.

fact: National Jewish Health lists ragweed among common Colorado allergens and says it and other allergenic weeds pollinate mostly in late summer and fall.
quote: Ragweed is another common allergen during gardening season. … Ragweed, like other allergenic weeds, pollinates mostly in the late summer and fall seasons.
source_label: National Jewish Health, 5 Common Colorado Allergens That Can Get in the Way of Gardening (published April 1, 2024)

fact: National Jewish Health says handling dried leaves, soil and bark mulch can trigger mold allergy, and that less contact with compost and rock mulch in place of bark mulch can make a big difference.
quote: Mold spores can cause people with mold allergies to have symptoms. If you find that your eyes are itching or that you’re coughing while handling things like dried leaves, soil, and bark mulch, you may have a mold allergy. People can also experience an irritant effect from these exposures. Reducing your contact with compost as much as possible and substituting rock mulch for bark mulch can make a big difference.
source_label: National Jewish Health, 5 Common Colorado Allergens That Can Get in the Way of Gardening (published April 1, 2024)

fact: National Jewish Health says indoor-outdoor cats and dogs collect pollen on their coats and carry it inside, and advises wiping pets down when they come in.
quote: Indoor/outdoor pets like cats and dogs like to roll around in the grass, accumulating all sorts of pollen on their coats. … Make sure to wipe down your pets when they come inside.
source_label: National Jewish Health, 5 Common Colorado Allergens That Can Get in the Way of Gardening (published April 1, 2024)

fact: CSU Extension says the usual assumption when a new lawn goes in is that Kentucky bluegrass must be planted, with little thought given to other species.
quote: Unfortunately, few people ask such questions before establishing a new turf. The basic assumption is that Kentucky bluegrass must be planted, and little consideration is given to alternative turfgrass species.
source_label: CSU Extension, CMG GardenNotes #561: Turfgrass Species Selection Guidelines (Koski, revised January 2012)

fact: CSU Extension says Kentucky bluegrass, perennial ryegrass and tall fescue all flower and try to set seedheads in spring, and that lowering the mowing height will not stop the flowering.
quote: All of the commonly used turfgrasses – Kentucky bluegrass, perennial ryegrass and tall fescue – will flower and attempt to produce seedheads in spring. … Lowering the mowing height will not eliminate flowering and is likely to stress the turf.
source_label: CSU Extension, PlantTalk Colorado 1557: Why Is Turf Sending Up So Many Seedheads?

fact: CSU Extension says male cottonwoods shed their pollen in April, that some towns restrict male trees because that pollen troubles allergy sufferers, and that the June cotton itself has no allergenic properties.
quote: Flowers on female trees, after being pollinated by wind-borne pollen from male trees in April, develop small green capsules that split open in June to shed small seeds carried by wind-borne “cotton”. … A few municipalities enact ordinances againstmale (“cotton less”) cottonwoods, because the April pollen causes problems for allergy sufferers. Although cotton can be a nuisance, it has no allergenic properties.
source_label: CSU Extension, PlantTalk Colorado 1758: Cottonwood Cotton
notes: "againstmale" is the page's own typo, quoted as printed. The page does not name the municipalities.

fact: A 2003 USDA Forest Service analysis found green ash was Fort Collins' most abundant street tree, at 22% of street trees, with American elm, Siberian elm and silver maple among the other important species.
quote: Green ash is the most abundant street tree species. It accounts for 22% of all street trees and produces 17% of all street tree benefits. Other important species by virtue of their size and numbers are Honeylocust, American elm, Hackberry, Siberian elm, Littleleaf linden, and Silver maple.
source_label: USDA Forest Service, Center for Urban Forest Research, Benefit-Cost Analysis of Fort Collins' Municipal Forest (McPherson et al., November 2003)
notes: An old count of city street trees only, not yard trees; emerald ash borer and removals since then will have changed it. The guide says the count is from 2003.

fact: The Asthma and Allergy Foundation of America says trees across the U.S. produce the most pollen from February through April, grass pollen is most common from April through early June, and weed pollen appears in late summer and fall.
quote: Throughout the U.S., trees produce the most pollen from February through April. … Grasses cause most late spring and summer pollen allergy symptoms. If you have a grass pollen allergy, where you live may also factor into when you have symptoms. Grass pollen is most common from April through early June. … Weed pollen appears in the late summer and fall.
source_label: Asthma and Allergy Foundation of America, Pollen Allergy (updated September 3, 2026)
notes: National timing, not Colorado's; the guide labels it as the national calendar.

fact: AAFA's list of trees that cause the most pollen allergy symptoms includes ash, box elder, cottonwood, elm, juniper and maple, and its list of common problem weeds includes burning bush, ragweed, Russian thistle, sagebrush and tumbleweed.
quote: Some of the trees that cause the most allergy symptoms are: Alder, Ash, Aspen, Beech, Birch, Box elder, Cedar, Cottonwood, Elm, Hickory, Juniper, Maple, Mulberry, Oak, Olive, Pecan, Poplar, Walnut, Willow … Common weeds that can cause symptoms include: Burning bush, Cocklebur, Lamb’s-quarters, Mugwort, Pigweed, Ragweed, Russian thistle, Sagebrush, Tumbleweed
source_label: Asthma and Allergy Foundation of America, Pollen Allergy (updated September 3, 2026)
notes: The page prints each tree and weed as a list item; the quote joins the items with commas.

fact: AAFA says flowering plants that spread pollen by insects, such as roses and cherry and pear trees, do not cause allergic rhinitis.
quote: Flowering plants that spread their pollen by insects − like roses and some trees, like cherry and pear trees − do not cause allergic rhinitis.
source_label: Asthma and Allergy Foundation of America, Pollen Allergy (updated September 3, 2026)

fact: AAFA says doctors usually diagnose a pollen allergy with 2 tests, a skin test and a specific IgE blood test.
quote: Doctors usually use 2 tests to diagnose a pollen allergy. … As with skin testing, a positive blood test to an allergen does not necessarily mean that an allergen caused your symptoms.
source_label: Asthma and Allergy Foundation of America, Pollen Allergy (updated September 3, 2026)

fact: The American Academy of Allergy, Asthma & Immunology says grass can also cause hives or welts, much less commonly than nasal symptoms, usually from actually touching the grass.
quote: People can also have skin rashes (hives or skin welts) after exposure to grasses, but this is much less common. … Rashes after exposure to grass usually are hives or welts. They are red, itchy and raised. Usually, actual contact with grass causes them.
source_label: American Academy of Allergy, Asthma & Immunology, Mowing Down Your Grass Allergies

fact: The American College of Allergy, Asthma and Immunology advises staying indoors when pollen counts peak, usually midmorning and early evening, and when wind is blowing pollen around.
quote: Stay indoors as much as possible when pollen counts are at their peak, usually during the midmorning and early evening (this may vary according to plant pollen), and when wind is blowing pollens around.
source_label: American College of Allergy, Asthma and Immunology, Hay Fever (Rhinitis) (updated February 21, 2023)

fact: ACAAI lists rubber, sunscreen, fragrant soaps and bleach among causes of contact dermatitis, says the rash can appear from a few hours to 10 days after contact, and says an allergist may use a patch test to find the cause.
quote: Poison ivy, jewelry made of certain metals (especially nickel or gold) and sunscreen all can cause contact dermatitis — a skin condition that results from exposure to something to which you’re either sensitive or allergic. Other common irritants or allergens include: Fragrant soaps, Rubber, Certain deodorants, Bleach, Hand sanitizers … These symptoms can range from mild to severe, and they can appear anywhere from a few hours to 10 days after coming into contact with the irritant or allergen. … To help your allergist identify potential causes of your contact dermatitis, record your activities and the items you think led to a reaction — or, if you’re unsure, simply list anything that may have touched your skin in the two days before your symptoms started. Your allergist might use a patch test to determine potential causes, such as rubber, fragrances or hair dye.
source_label: American College of Allergy, Asthma and Immunology, Contact Dermatitis (updated April 13, 2022)
notes: The page prints the irritants as list items; the quote joins them with commas.

fact: Washington State's Department of Health says turf blades are commonly polyethylene, polypropylene or nylon, that the secondary backing coating can be latex or polyurethane, and that people using turf fields aren't likely to be exposed to the backing.
quote: The grass blades are commonly made from materials such as polyethylene, polypropylene, and nylon. … The secondary backing is a coating on the back of the turf that helps create weather durability. Types of secondary backing material can include latex and polyurethane. Unlike the infill material, chemical exposure from backing material is less studied. People using these fields aren’t likely to be exposed to backing material, but workers who install, maintain, and remove fields handle backing material
source_label: Washington State Department of Health, Artificial Turf

fact: Washington's health department says common infills include sand, tire crumb rubber and cork, and that some studies found plant-based infills had the fewest chemicals of concern but could pose hazards from mold, allergens and inhaled fibers.
quote: Common infill materials include sand, tire crumb rubber, and cork. … Tire crumb rubber is created from shredding recycled tires and contains many chemicals. … For example, some studies concluded that plant-based alternatives were found to contain the fewest chemicals of concern but could pose other hazards related to mold, allergens, and inhalation of fibers.
source_label: Washington State Department of Health, Artificial Turf

fact: Washington's health department says turf burns are skin abrasions from friction against the fibers, recommends clothing that covers the skin, and says hot turf raises concerns of burns and blisters.
quote: Non-chemical safety issues include turf burns which are skin abrasions caused by friction of the skin on artificial grass fibers. Turf burns can happen by sliding or falling during any sporting activities. … For artificial turf users, high surface temperatures lead to concerns of burns, blisters, dehydration, and other heat related stress or illnesses. … To avoid turf burns, we recommend people wear clothes that don’t expose too much skin while playing on artificial turf fields, including long sleeve shirts, long pants, and long socks.
source_label: Washington State Department of Health, Artificial Turf

fact: The Synthetic Turf Council's 2013 buyer's guide says turf backings are coated with polyurethane, hot melt polyolefin or latex, and that North American makers were using polyurethane and hot melt polyolefin.
quote: The back of the synthetic grass is coated with secondary backing materials to lock the fibers in place (tuft bind). Several different coating materials are used, including Polyurethane (PU), Hot Melt Polyolefin (HMP), and Latex. North American synthetic grass manufacturers currently use PU and HMP.
source_label: Synthetic Turf Council, Considerations When Buying Synthetic Grass for Landscape Use (September 2013)
notes: "Currently" is as of the 2013 printing; imported turf may differ. The guide tells readers to ask for the coating on the spec sheet.

fact: The American Academy of Allergy, Asthma & Immunology says latex allergy is a reaction to proteins in natural rubber latex from rubber trees, that latex paints contain no natural rubber latex protein, and that synthetic latex gloves contain no natural latex.
quote: Natural rubber latex, a milky fluid found in rubber trees, is used to make some gloves, condoms, balloons, rubber bands, erasers and toys. … It may be surprising, but latex paints do not contain any natural rubber latex protein. … With latex allergy, it overreacts by producing antibodies called Immunoglobulin E (IgE) that can react with contaminating proteins found in the natural rubber latex. … Synthetic latex gloves do not contain natural latex and are another option.
source_label: American Academy of Allergy, Asthma & Immunology, Latex Allergy

fact: Motz, which sells a walnut-shell infill, says the product was designed by a parent of a nut-allergic child and that a heating process removes residual walnut allergens from the shells.
quote: Most organic infill products today are made from things like walnut shells, wood fiber, coconut fiber, olive pits, and rice husks. … and was designed by a parent with a nut-allergic child. During Safeshell’s production process, any residual allergens that may have carried over from the walnut onto the shell are removed using a proprietary, chemical-free heating process.
source_label: Motz, Organic Infill Can Make Your Artificial Turf More Sustainable: 7 Things to Know (October 4, 2021; modified September 28, 2023)
notes: The maker's own claim about its product, not an independent test; the guide presents it that way and sends readers to their allergist.

fact: A PubMed search on September 25, 2026 for artificial turf dermatitis returned no results, as did searches for artificial turf allergy, synthetic turf allergy and artificial turf urticaria.
quote: No results were found.
source_label: PubMed, U.S. National Library of Medicine: search for artificial turf dermatitis, run September 25, 2026
notes: Also run the same day with no results: ?term=artificial+turf+allergy, ?term=synthetic+turf+allergy, ?term=artificial+turf+urticaria. An empty search is not proof that no reaction has ever happened; the guide says only that it found no published case.
